questions.title: The Central Limit Theorem and the Standard Error of the Mean
questions.prompt: You're estimating the mean daily return of a stock from one year of daily log returns. Walk me through what the Central Limit Theorem tells you about the sampling distribution of that estimate, and explain why doubling your sample size does not halve your uncertainty.
questions.modelAnswer: The Law of Large Numbers guarantees the sample mean of daily returns converges to the true mean as the sample grows, but it says nothing about the shape of the remaining uncertainty. The Central Limit Theorem fills that gap: for i.i.d. observations with finite mean mu and finite variance sigma^2, sqrt(n)*(X_bar - mu)/sigma converges in distribution to N(0,1), so for large n the sample mean itself is approximately X_bar ~ N(mu, sigma^2/n). Critically, this holds regardless of the shape of the daily return distribution (skewed, fat-tailed, whatever) as long as the variance is finite. The standard deviation of that sampling distribution, sigma/sqrt(n), is called the standard error of the mean, and it shrinks with the square root of n, not linearly. That means to cut the uncertainty in half you need four times as much data, not twice as much -- which is exactly why precisely estimating a mean daily return from historical data is so hard: daily volatility is large relative to the mean you're trying to pin down, and the sqrt(n) scaling makes that gap close only very slowly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it the way I actually think about it when someone hands me a 'the average daily return is X%' claim. The Law of Large Numbers is the reason I believe averaging is a sensible thing to do at all -- with enough data, the sample mean gets close to the truth. But the CLT is the more useful tool day to day, because it tells me how precise that estimate is: the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal with standard deviation sigma over root n, and that holds even though daily returns themselves are clearly not normal -- they're fat-tailed and a bit skewed. The part that trips people up, and that I'd flag explicitly, is the square-root scaling. If I have a year of data and want to cut my standard error in half, I don't need two years, I need four. That's the practical reason a 'statistically significant' mean-return estimate from a few years of daily data should always be treated with some suspicion -- the standard error is often embarrassingly large relative to the number you're estimating.
questions.example: With a daily volatility of 1.5% and 252 trading days in a year, the standard error of the annual mean-return estimate is 0.015/sqrt(252) ≈ 0.00094, or about 0.094% per day -- often larger than the mean return itself, which is why a single year of daily data rarely lets you reject the null hypothesis that the true mean return is zero.
commonMistakes: Assuming the CLT requires the underlying daily returns to already be normally distributed, rather than understanding it's the average that becomes approximately normal
Confusing the Law of Large Numbers (the mean converges) with the Central Limit Theorem (the shape and rate of that convergence)
Assuming standard error shrinks proportionally with sample size instead of with its square root
Forgetting that the classical CLT requires finite variance, which can fail for extremely heavy-tailed return series
keyPoints: LLN says the sample mean converges to the true mean; CLT describes the shape of the remaining uncertainty
sqrt(n)*(X_bar - mu)/sigma -> N(0,1) holds for any finite-variance i.i.d. distribution, not just normal data
Standard error of the mean is sigma/sqrt(n)
Halving the standard error requires 4x the data, not 2x
This is why mean-return estimates from daily data are often imprecise even over multi-year windows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the CLT correctly, including that it holds regardless of the underlying distribution's shape
Explains the sqrt(n) standard-error scaling and its practical consequence
Distinguishes the Law of Large Numbers from the Central Limit Theorem
Clarity and use of a concrete framing

questions.title: Why Model Returns, Not Prices
questions.prompt: A junior analyst wants to fit an ARMA model directly to a stock's daily closing-price series. Explain why that's a problem, and what 'stationarity' actually means in this context.
questions.modelAnswer: A time series is weakly (covariance) stationary if, for all t, it has a constant mean, a constant variance, and an autocovariance that depends only on the lag between two points, not on calendar time itself. Raw stock prices violate this badly: they trend over time (so the mean isn't constant) and their variance tends to grow or shift across regimes. A price series behaves like a random walk, which has a unit root -- shocks never decay, and the variance of the level grows without bound as time passes. Fitting ARMA, GARCH, or almost any classical time-series model to a non-stationary series produces unreliable, often nonsensical parameter estimates and spurious-looking fits, because those models assume the statistical properties they're estimating (mean, variance, autocorrelation structure) are stable over the estimation window. The fix is to work with log returns instead of prices: differencing the log price series removes the trend and typically produces a series that passes a stationarity test (such as the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test) decisively, which is why virtually every model in quantitative finance is built on returns, not price levels.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop the analyst before they run the model and ask: does this series look like it has the same statistical behavior in year one as it does in year five? For a raw price series, obviously not -- it trends, and its volatility shifts around. That's non-stationarity, and it's not a minor technicality; ARMA's whole machinery assumes constant mean and a lag-only autocovariance structure, so fitting it to a trending price series gives you garbage parameter estimates that happen to look plausible. The fix I'd actually make them do is take log returns instead -- differencing the log price kills the trend and, in my experience, almost always turns a series that fails an ADF test into one that passes it cleanly. I'd also flag that this isn't just an ARMA issue; GARCH, cointegration tests, basically everything downstream in this kind of research assumes some form of stationarity, so getting this step right first saves a lot of debugging later.
commonMistakes: Treating 'stationary' and 'normally distributed' as the same property
Assuming a model 'fitting' without errors means the stationarity assumption was satisfied
Not realizing that returns, not prices, are the quantity that's actually of interest anyway -- nobody invests to own a price level
Forgetting that even engineered features (rolling sums, cumulative fundamentals) can inherit the same non-stationarity problem
keyPoints: Weak stationarity: constant mean, constant variance, autocovariance depends only on lag
Raw price levels trend and have shifting variance, so they fail stationarity
A price series behaves like a random walk / unit-root process -- shocks never decay
Log returns are (usually) stationary, which is why models are built on returns, not prices
The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test is the standard way to check this in practice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives the correct definition of weak stationarity
Explains why raw prices violate it and why returns typically satisfy it
Mentions a concrete consequence of fitting a model to non-stationary data

questions.title: Computing Log Returns and Why Time-Additivity Matters
questions.prompt: Given a pandas Series of daily closing prices called `prices`, write the code to compute both simple returns and log returns. Then explain why a quant researcher building a multi-day cumulative-return feature would reach for log returns instead of simple returns.
questions.code:
import pandas as pd

prices = pd.Series([100.0, 102.0, 101.0, 105.0, 110.0])
questions.modelAnswer: Simple returns are computed with `prices.pct_change()`, giving (P_t - P_{t-1})/P_{t-1}. Log returns are computed with `np.log(prices).diff()` (equivalently `np.log(prices / prices.shift(1))`), giving ln(P_t/P_{t-1}). The key property that makes log returns the default choice for a multi-day feature is time-additivity: the log return over several periods is exactly the sum of the one-period log returns, r_(t-k,t) = r_t + r_{t-1} + ... + r_{t-k+1}. That means a '5-day cumulative return' feature can be built by summing five daily log returns with a rolling `.sum()`, which is both simpler and numerically cleaner than the multiplicative compounding simple returns require, (1+R_1)*(1+R_2)*...*(1+R_n) - 1. Simple returns have their own useful property -- cross-sectional (portfolio) additivity, since a portfolio's return is the weighted average of its holdings' simple returns -- but that's the wrong property for a single-asset, multi-period feature, which is exactly the case here.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd just write it directly: `simple_returns = prices.pct_change()` and `log_returns = np.log(prices).diff()`. For the 'why log returns' part, the honest answer is almost always time-additivity -- if I want a 5-day momentum feature, I can just take a rolling sum of daily log returns instead of multiplying five (1+R) terms together, which is cleaner to compute and avoids any multiplicative compounding mistakes. I'd also mention the flip side so it doesn't sound like log returns are always correct: if I were instead building a portfolio-level return from several holdings at one point in time, I'd want simple returns, because those are the ones that add up correctly across assets in a weighted average. Picking the wrong one for the wrong axis -- time versus assets -- is a classic beginner mistake.
questions.example: cum_growth_from_log = np.exp(log_returns.cumsum()) and cum_growth_from_simple = (1 + simple_returns).cumprod() should match up to floating-point noise over the same window -- a good sanity check that both were computed correctly.
commonMistakes: Summing simple returns instead of compounding them multiplicatively, which overstates true cumulative growth
Using log returns to aggregate across assets in a portfolio at a single point in time, where simple returns are the correct additive quantity
Forgetting the first value of either series is NaN and needs to be dropped before feeding it into a model
Not recognizing that for small moves the two return types are numerically very close, which can hide a real bug for a while
keyPoints: `pct_change()` for simple returns, `np.log(prices).diff()` for log returns
Log returns are time-additive: multi-period log return is the sum of one-period log returns
Simple returns are cross-sectionally additive: a portfolio's return is the weighted average of its holdings' simple returns
A multi-day feature should use log returns and a rolling sum, not multiplicative compounding of simple returns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct pandas/NumPy code for both return types
Correctly explains time-additivity as the reason to prefer log returns here
Correctly distinguishes when simple returns are actually the right choice

questions.title: Computing Portfolio Variance as a Quadratic Form
questions.prompt: You're given a 3-asset covariance matrix `Sigma` as a NumPy array and a weight vector `w`. Write the NumPy code to compute the portfolio's variance, and explain in one sentence why that result is guaranteed to be non-negative no matter what weights you choose.
questions.modelAnswer: Portfolio variance is the quadratic form `portfolio_var = w @ Sigma @ w`. This is guaranteed non-negative because a covariance matrix is always symmetric positive semi-definite: for any weight vector w, w^T*Sigma*w equals Var(w^T*X), the variance of the weighted combination of the underlying asset returns, and a variance can never be negative. Note the common mistake of writing `w * Sigma * w`, which is elementwise multiplication on mismatched shapes and not the matrix-algebra operation at all -- `@` must be used for matrix-vector multiplication in NumPy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write `w @ Sigma @ w` and leave it at that for the code. For the 'why is it always non-negative' part, the clean way to say it is that w^T*Sigma*w is literally the variance of the portfolio's return, Var(w^T*X), and variances are never negative by definition -- so the positive semi-definiteness of a covariance matrix isn't some separate fact you have to prove, it falls straight out of what the matrix actually represents. I'd also flag the NumPy gotcha here, because it's the single most common mistake I see: people write `w * Sigma * w` using `*`, which is elementwise, not `@`. That either errors out on shape mismatch or silently gives you a meaningless array instead of a scalar.
commonMistakes: Using `*` (elementwise multiplication) instead of `@` (matrix multiplication)
Forgetting to flatten the result to a scalar when weights are passed as a column vector
Explaining positive semi-definiteness as an abstract linear-algebra fact rather than connecting it to 'this number is literally a variance'
Not checking that `Sigma` is actually symmetric before trusting downstream calculations built on it
keyPoints: Portfolio variance is the quadratic form w^T * Sigma * w
Use `@` for matrix/vector multiplication in NumPy, never `*`
A covariance matrix is always symmetric positive semi-definite because w^T*Sigma*w = Var(w^T*X) >= 0
This single fact underlies mean-variance portfolio optimization and PCA

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct NumPy code using `@`
Correctly explains why the result is non-negative, tying it to the definition of variance
Clarity

questions.title: A Backtest That Looks Too Good to Be True
questions.prompt: A new intern shows you a backtest of a simple moving-average crossover strategy with a Sharpe ratio of 4.5. Before getting excited, what are the first two or three things you'd check?
questions.modelAnswer: A Sharpe ratio that high on a simple strategy is a red flag, not a reason for excitement, and the first checks should target the most common causes. First, look-ahead bias: does every signal and feature in the backtest use only information that would actually have been available at that point in time, or did something (an index membership list, a restated fundamental, a same-day closing price used to both generate and execute the signal) sneak in from the future? Second, survivorship bias: was the universe built from today's list of surviving assets, projected backward, silently excluding companies or funds that were delisted or went bankrupt along the way? Third, ask how many variants of this strategy (different moving-average windows, different thresholds) were tried before this one was shown to you -- if dozens were tested and only the best one is being reported, that's a multiple-testing problem, and an impressively high Sharpe ratio is exactly what you'd expect to see from pure chance across enough trials, even with zero real skill in any of them.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, my gut reaction to a 4.5 Sharpe on a moving-average crossover is suspicion, not excitement -- that's an extraordinary number for a strategy that simple. The first thing I'd ask is whether the backtest could be peeking into the future anywhere: is the signal computed using only prices available up to that bar's close, or did a rolling window accidentally include the current (or a future) bar? Second, I'd ask about the universe -- is this tested only on stocks that are still around today, which would quietly exclude every company that blew up along the way and flatter the result? And third, and this is the one interns usually haven't thought about yet, I'd ask how many parameter combinations were tried to land on this specific one. If it's the best of fifty window lengths tried, a great-looking Sharpe is just what you'd expect from noise alone, and reporting only the winner without saying how many were tried is a classic way research fools itself.
commonMistakes: Getting excited about a high Sharpe ratio before checking for look-ahead or survivorship bias
Not asking how many strategy variants were tried before this one was selected
Assuming the backtest costs (if any) were modeled realistically without checking
Treating 'the backtest runs without errors' as evidence the result is trustworthy
keyPoints: An unusually high Sharpe ratio on a simple strategy should trigger scrutiny, not celebration
Check for look-ahead bias: does every feature only use information that was actually available at that time
Check for survivorship bias: does the universe include assets that were delisted or went bankrupt
Ask how many strategy variants were tried -- multiple testing inflates the apparent best result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies look-ahead bias as a check
Identifies survivorship bias as a check
Identifies multiple testing / number of variants tried as a check
Correctly frames a high Sharpe ratio as suspicious rather than exciting

questions.title: Why Hardcoded File Paths Hurt a Research Codebase
questions.prompt: Ten different notebooks in your research repo each call `pd.read_parquet()` with a hardcoded path to a vendor file. What goes wrong with this pattern over time, and what's the basic fix?
questions.modelAnswer: Hardcoding a file path into every notebook that needs the data means the loading and cleaning logic is duplicated ten times. The moment the source changes -- a new vendor, a renamed column, a moved file -- every one of those call sites has to be found and fixed individually, and any two of them that handle a quirk (a timezone, a column name, a missing-value convention) even slightly differently will silently produce different numbers from what's supposed to be 'the same' data. The fix is a thin research data layer: a function like `load_prices(universe, start, end)` that hides the actual source (file path, column names, timezone handling) behind a stable interface, so every notebook calls the same function instead of re-implementing the read-and-clean logic. That also makes it trivial to add caching in one place, since every caller now goes through the same code path.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those things that looks totally fine on day one and becomes a real mess by month three. If ten notebooks all hardcode the same file path, you don't actually have one source of truth -- you have ten copies of the loading logic that happen to currently agree. The day the vendor renames a column or the file moves, you're hunting through ten notebooks instead of fixing one function. My actual fix is always the same: write a `load_prices(universe, start, end)`-style function once, have it handle the messy stuff -- column names, timezones, whatever the raw file's quirks are -- and make every notebook call that function instead of touching the file directly. Then if the source changes, I fix it in one place and every notebook downstream just keeps working.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a minor style preference rather than a real source of silent data inconsistency
Fixing the hardcoded path problem by search-and-replace across notebooks instead of introducing a shared function
Not normalizing column names, dtypes, and timezones consistently across different data sources
Forgetting that a stable interface also makes caching trivial to add later, in one place
keyPoints: Duplicated hardcoded paths mean duplicated loading/cleaning logic across every call site
A source change requires fixing every call site individually, and inconsistent handling causes silently different results
The fix is a stable interface function (e.g. load_prices) that hides the source behind a consistent contract
This also makes caching and future source changes much easier to manage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the duplication/inconsistency problem clearly
Proposes a stable-interface function as the fix

questions.title: Explaining a Sharpe Ratio to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A member of the firm's investor-relations team, who has no statistics background, asks you what a 'Sharpe ratio of 1.2' actually means and whether it's good. How do you explain it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids formulas entirely and leads with the intuition: the Sharpe ratio measures how much return you're getting for the amount of bumpiness, or risk, you had to tolerate to get it -- it's return per unit of volatility, not just return on its own. A Sharpe of 1.2 means that, historically, the strategy's average excess return each year has been about 1.2 times its own year-to-year volatility, which is a solid, respectable figure for most systematic strategies (very few strategies sustain much above 2 for long, and many real strategies run well below 1). The honest caveat worth adding is that a Sharpe ratio alone doesn't tell you about tail risk or how the strategy behaves in a crash, which is a reasonable point to make rather than letting the single number stand in for the whole risk picture.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start without any math at all: 'it's a way of measuring how much return you got for how much risk you had to take to get it, not just the return by itself.' Then I'd give them a number to anchor on -- most systematic strategies that are considered genuinely good land somewhere between 0.5 and 1.5, so 1.2 is solidly in the respectable range, not spectacular but not weak either. I'd be careful not to oversell it, though -- I'd also say plainly that Sharpe ratio doesn't capture everything, especially tail risk, so a strategy can have a perfectly fine Sharpe ratio and still have a bad month if the market does something unusual. I think that honesty actually builds more trust with a non-technical stakeholder than a confident-sounding number alone would.
commonMistakes: Leading with the formula (mean excess return divided by standard deviation) instead of the intuition
Implying a single number like Sharpe ratio captures the whole risk picture
Failing to give a benchmark (what counts as a 'good' Sharpe ratio in practice) for context
Using jargon like 'risk-adjusted' without unpacking what that actually means
keyPoints: Sharpe ratio is return per unit of risk (volatility), not return alone
Gives a practical benchmark for what counts as a reasonable value
Avoids formulas and jargon when explaining to a non-technical audience
Honestly notes the metric's limitation (it doesn't capture tail risk)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the concept in plain, non-technical language
Gives useful context for what counts as a good value

questions.title: When Your Research Hypothesis Turns Out to Be Wrong
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you were confident a signal or hypothesis would work, built it out, and the data told you otherwise. How did you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names a specific hypothesis, states plainly what the researcher expected and why, describes the actual result that contradicted it, and explains what they did next -- rather than quietly abandoning the idea or forcing the data to agree. The best answers show the researcher stating the hypothesis and success criteria before looking at results (so the negative finding isn't just hindsight), checking whether the negative result was a real finding or a bug in the pipeline, and then documenting the negative result rather than burying it, since a well-documented null result saves someone else from re-testing the same idea later.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell this as a short, specific story rather than a general principle. I'd name the actual hypothesis I had going in, be honest about why I was confident, describe concretely what the data showed instead, and then focus most of the answer on what I did next -- did I double-check it wasn't a bug, did I write it down somewhere so the next person doesn't waste a week re-testing the same idea, did I update how I think about that kind of signal going forward. I think the thing an interviewer is actually listening for here is whether I treat a wrong hypothesis as useful information or as a personal failure -- the honest answer is it's useful information, and pretending otherwise is a worse habit than being wrong in the first place.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague, generic answer with no specific hypothesis or result
Describing the failure but not what was done afterward (verifying it wasn't a bug, documenting it)
Sounding defensive about having been wrong, rather than treating it as a normal part of research
Claiming the hypothesis was secretly 'right all along' with minor caveats, rather than genuinely updating
keyPoints: States a specific hypothesis and why it seemed reasonable beforehand
Describes the actual contradicting result honestly
Verifies the negative result wasn't itself a pipeline bug before accepting it
Documents or acts on the negative finding rather than quietly dropping it

Shows intellectual honesty about being wrong

questions.title: Skewness, Kurtosis, and Why Equity Returns Aren't Normal
questions.prompt: A colleague says 'daily stock returns are basically normal, so a 3-sigma move should be extremely rare.' Using skewness and kurtosis, explain why that's a risky assumption for equity returns.
questions.modelAnswer: Skewness is the standardized third central moment, E[(X-mu)^3]/sigma^3, measuring asymmetry; a symmetric distribution like the normal has skewness 0. Kurtosis is the standardized fourth central moment, E[(X-mu)^4]/sigma^4, measuring tail weight; the normal distribution has kurtosis exactly 3, so 'excess kurtosis' (kurtosis minus 3) above zero means fatter tails than normal. Equity returns typically show negative skew (crashes are sharper than rallies) and substantial positive excess kurtosis (fat tails) -- which means a 3-sigma-or-larger move happens far more often in real markets than a normal model would predict, because the normal model systematically underprices the probability mass sitting in the tails. Treating returns as normal because they 'look roughly bell-shaped' in the middle ignores exactly the part of the distribution -- the tails -- that matters most for risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on that claim directly: yes, daily returns look roughly bell-curved in the middle, but the normal distribution's whole value is in predicting how often extreme values occur, and that's exactly where it fails for equities. Skewness tells you the distribution leans -- equity returns usually skew negative, meaning big down moves are more extreme than big up moves. Kurtosis tells you about the tails specifically, and real return series routinely show excess kurtosis well above zero, meaning 3-, 4-, even 5-sigma moves happen on a real trading desk far more often than 'extremely rare' would suggest under a true normal model. I'd want anyone sizing risk off a normal assumption to know this gap exists before they trust a VaR number built on it.
commonMistakes: Treating 'returns look bell-shaped in the middle' as evidence the normal assumption is safe for tail risk
Forgetting the normal distribution's kurtosis is 3, not 0 -- so 'excess kurtosis' is kurtosis minus 3, not kurtosis itself
Assuming skewness and kurtosis measure the same thing (shape overall) rather than two distinct properties (asymmetry vs. tail weight)
keyPoints: Skewness measures asymmetry; equities are typically negatively skewed
Kurtosis measures tail weight; normal kurtosis is 3, so excess kurtosis > 0 means fat tails
Fat tails mean large moves happen far more often than a normal model predicts
A distribution can look bell-shaped in the middle while still being dangerously wrong in the tails

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines skewness and kurtosis
Correctly states the normal distribution's kurtosis is 3, not 0

questions.title: What an Eigenvector of a Covariance Matrix Actually Means
questions.prompt: You compute the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a 5-asset covariance matrix. In plain terms, what does the top eigenvector represent, and what does its eigenvalue tell you?
questions.modelAnswer: An eigenvector v of the covariance matrix Sigma, with eigenvalue lambda, satisfies Sigma*v = lambda*v: applying Sigma to v only scales it, never rotates it. Interpreted as portfolio weights, v represents a specific combination of the 5 assets -- a direction in 'return space' -- and because Sigma is symmetric positive semi-definite, v^T*Sigma*v (the variance of that portfolio) equals exactly lambda. So the top eigenvector is the particular combination of the 5 assets that captures the single largest amount of variance achievable from any such combination, and its eigenvalue is literally that amount of variance. This is the exact mechanism Principal Component Analysis exploits: the eigenvectors of a covariance matrix are orthogonal directions of risk, ranked by how much variance each one explains.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain it: an eigenvector here isn't one of the five assets, it's a specific portfolio -- a particular weighting across all five. What makes it special is that Sigma just stretches that exact weighting vector without rotating it into some different combination, and the amount of stretch is the eigenvalue. Because of how covariance matrices work, that stretch factor is literally the variance of the portfolio you'd get from using those weights. So the top eigenvector is 'the single riskiest independent combination of these five assets you could construct,' and its eigenvalue tells you exactly how much variance that combination carries -- which is also exactly the first step of running PCA on this same matrix.
commonMistakes: Thinking an eigenvector corresponds to a single asset rather than a weighted combination of all of them
Forgetting the eigenvalue IS the variance of the portfolio defined by that eigenvector, not just an abstract scaling number
Not realizing the sign/orientation of an eigenvector is arbitrary -- any nonzero scalar multiple is still a valid eigenvector
keyPoints: Sigma*v = lambda*v: v is a direction Sigma only scales, not rotates
Interpreted as weights, v is a specific portfolio combination of the assets
The eigenvalue lambda equals v^T*Sigma*v, the variance of that portfolio
The top eigenvector/eigenvalue pair is the single largest-variance direction in the data
This is the exact mechanism PCA uses to decompose risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states the eigenvalue equation and its geometric meaning
Correctly interprets the eigenvector as a portfolio combination

questions.title: Why Prices Are Modeled Lognormal but Returns Are Modeled Normal
questions.prompt: Explain why quant models typically assume an asset's price is lognormally distributed while its log-return is normally distributed, rather than modeling the price itself as normal.
questions.modelAnswer: A normal random variable can take any value, including negative ones, which makes it a poor model for a price -- a stock price can never go below zero, so modeling price itself as normal would assign positive probability to an impossible outcome. The fix is to model the LOG of the price as normal instead: if Y=ln(S) ~ N(mu, sigma^2), then S itself is lognormally distributed and, by construction, always strictly positive, no matter how negative Y gets. This is also exactly consistent with modeling log-returns, ln(S_t/S_{t-1}), as approximately normal: if each log-return is normal, the cumulative log-price is a sum of normals (hence also normal), and the price itself is lognormal at every horizon -- this is the distributional backbone of geometric Brownian motion and the Black-Scholes framework.
questions.professionalAnswer: The short version: prices can't be negative, but a normal distribution doesn't know that and would happily put real probability mass below zero if you modeled price directly with it. So instead you push the normal assumption one level down, onto the log of the price -- or equivalently, onto log-returns -- which automatically keeps the price itself positive no matter what, since exponentiating any real number, however negative, still gives a positive price. I'd also flag the honest caveat here, which later material gets into: real log-returns aren't perfectly normal either -- they're fatter-tailed and a bit skewed -- so lognormal-for-prices is best treated as a clean baseline model, not the final word on how prices actually behave.
commonMistakes: Modeling the price level itself as normal, which allows impossible negative prices
Assuming lognormal and normal distributions have the same shape, just shifted
Treating 'returns are modeled normal' as an exact empirical fact rather than a baseline assumption with known fat-tail violations
keyPoints: A normal distribution allows negative values, which is wrong for a price
If ln(S) is normal, S is lognormal and always positive by construction
This connects directly to modeling log-returns as normal, since log-price is a sum of log-returns
Real log-returns deviate from exact normality (fat tails, skew) -- this is a baseline, not a perfect description

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why normal is wrong for price levels specifically
Correctly connects lognormal prices to normal log-returns

questions.title: The Markov Property, in Plain Terms
questions.prompt: A trader claims a stock's credit rating migration only depends on its current rating, not on how it got there or how long it's been there. What property is this, and how would you represent it mathematically with a small ratings example?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the Markov property: P(X_(n+1)=j | X_n=i, X_(n-1), ..., X_0) = P(X_(n+1)=j | X_n=i) -- the future depends on the past only through the present state, not the full history that led there. A rating-migration model is naturally represented with a transition matrix P, where P_ij is the probability of moving from rating i to rating j in one step; every row of P sums to 1, since from any rating the firm must go somewhere (including staying put). For a small 3-state example (say AA, BBB, Default, with Default absorbing), P might have rows like [0.95, 0.04, 0.01] for AA, reflecting that the probability of moving from AA next period depends only on being AA right now, regardless of whether the firm was AAA or BB two periods ago.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name it directly: that's the Markov property, and it's a genuinely strong claim -- it says today's rating is literally all the information that matters, full stop, not 'mostly' or 'approximately' all the information. The natural way to write this down is a transition matrix: one row per current rating, one column per next rating, each row summing to 1 because wherever you start, you have to land somewhere next period, even if 'somewhere' is just staying in the same rating. A toy example with three ratings and a default state that's absorbing (once you default you stay defaulted) is the cleanest way to make this concrete, and it's exactly the structure real credit-migration models are built on.
commonMistakes: Confusing the Markov property with full independence between time steps (it's not independent, it depends on the current state)
Forgetting a valid transition matrix's rows must each sum to 1
Assuming the Markov property means there's no structure at all, rather than structure that's fully captured by the current state

A transition matrix P has P_ij = probability of moving from state i to state j
Every row of a valid transition matrix sums to 1
An absorbing state (like default) has a row that stays entirely in itself

questions.title: The Random Walk Hypothesis and Market Efficiency
questions.prompt: Explain the connection between the random-walk model of stock prices and the (weak-form) Efficient Market Hypothesis. If someone shows you a profitable pattern in daily closing prices, how does this connection make you skeptical by default?
questions.modelAnswer: Under the (weak-form) Efficient Market Hypothesis, current prices already reflect all information contained in past prices, so the only thing that should move a price going forward is genuinely new information -- which, by definition, is unpredictable. That's exactly an i.i.d. increment added to the previous price: a random walk, S_n = S_0 + sum of i.i.d. steps. This connection is why, under reasonably efficient markets, raw price levels are expected to behave like a random walk (variance growing linearly in n, standard deviation growing like sqrt(n)) rather than following any predictable pattern. If someone shows a 'pattern' in historical closing prices that appears profitable, the EMH-random-walk connection is exactly why the default reaction should be skepticism: if the pattern were real and known, it should already have been traded away and arbitraged out of existence -- so the burden of proof is on showing the pattern survives rigorous out-of-sample testing, not on disproving it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The connection is almost definitional once you see it: EMH says a price already reflects everything knowable, so only brand-new information should move it, and brand-new information is unpredictable by definition -- which is exactly what a random-walk increment is. That's why, if I'm handed a backtest claiming some clean, exploitable pattern in past closing prices, my default reaction isn't excitement, it's suspicion: if that pattern were real and known, market participants trading on it should have already arbitraged it away, which is the whole mechanism that keeps markets close to efficient in the first place. I'd want to see it survive genuine out-of-sample testing before taking it seriously, not just see a clean-looking chart.
commonMistakes: Treating the random walk connection as proof markets are literally unpredictable in every sense (that's the much stronger strong-form EMH claim)
Forgetting a random walk can still have nonzero drift even under EMH, as compensation for risk
Not applying appropriate default skepticism to a 'discovered' pattern in historical prices
keyPoints: EMH: prices reflect available information, so only new (unpredictable) information should move them
Unpredictable price changes = i.i.d. increments = a random walk
This connection is why weak-form efficient markets should show little linear predictability in past prices
A 'found' pattern in past prices warrants default skepticism until proven out-of-sample

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the EMH-to-random-walk connection
Correctly frames why a 'found' pattern should be treated skeptically
Avoids overstating EMH as proving markets are unpredictable in every sense

questions.title: What a p-value of 0.03 Actually Means
questions.prompt: A researcher says, 'our strategy's p-value was 0.03, so there's a 97% chance it has real alpha.' What's wrong with that statement, and what does the p-value actually tell you?
questions.modelAnswer: A p-value is defined as P(observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed | the null hypothesis is true) -- it is a statement about how surprising the data would be IF there were truly no effect, not a statement about the probability that the null (or the alternative) is actually true. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean there's a 97% chance the strategy has real alpha; it means that if the strategy truly had zero alpha, there'd only be a 3% chance of seeing a result this extreme by chance alone. Converting a p-value directly into 'probability the hypothesis is true' is one of the single most common and consequential misunderstandings in applied statistics, and it ignores the prior probability that the strategy had real alpha in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct this plainly: a p-value of 0.03 is not '97% chance the alpha is real.' What it actually says is narrower and more mechanical -- if the true alpha were exactly zero, you'd only expect to see a result this extreme about 3% of the time by chance. Those are very different statements, because the p-value is calculated under the assumption that the null is true; it doesn't tell you the probability that assumption itself is correct. People reach for the '97% chance it's real' framing because it's more satisfying, but it's simply not what the number means, and conflating the two is exactly the kind of mistake that leads a team to overtrust a mediocre result.
commonMistakes: Treating the p-value as the probability the null hypothesis is true
Treating 1 minus the p-value as the probability the alternative hypothesis is true
Ignoring that the p-value is calculated under the assumption the null IS true, not as an unconditional probability statement
keyPoints: p-value = P(observed-or-more-extreme statistic | H0 is true)
It is NOT P(H0 is true) and NOT P(H1 is true)
0.03 means: if the null were true, this result (or more extreme) would happen 3% of the time by chance
This is one of the most common statistical misinterpretations in applied research

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the correct, precise definition of a p-value
Clearly explains why the '97% chance it's real' framing is wrong

questions.title: What 'OLS is BLUE' Actually Promises
questions.prompt: You run a CAPM regression and get an estimated beta. A colleague asks whether OLS is the 'best' way to estimate it. What does the Gauss-Markov theorem actually guarantee, and what does it NOT guarantee?
questions.modelAnswer: Under the five Gauss-Markov assumptions (linearity, strict exogeneity, no perfect multicollinearity, homoscedasticity, no autocorrelation), the Gauss-Markov theorem guarantees OLS is BLUE: the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator -- meaning among every estimator that is both linear in y and unbiased, OLS has the smallest variance. It does NOT guarantee OLS is the best possible estimator among all estimators, including nonlinear or deliberately biased ones (a shrinkage estimator can sometimes do better in total error). It also does NOT guarantee correct standard errors if homoscedasticity or no-autocorrelation fail -- OLS's point estimate of beta stays unbiased, but the reported standard errors become wrong, which breaks any hypothesis test built on them unless robust (White or Newey-West) standard errors are used instead. And it says nothing about whether the regression itself is economically meaningful.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific about exactly what 'BLUE' promises, because it's narrower than it sounds. It means: among linear, unbiased estimators, OLS has the lowest variance -- that's a real, useful guarantee, but it's conditional on five assumptions holding. What it doesn't promise: that OLS beats every possible estimator, including ones that trade a little bias for a lot less variance; and critically, if homoscedasticity or no-autocorrelation fail, the beta estimate itself often stays unbiased, but the standard errors you'd use to judge statistical significance become unreliable -- which is exactly why you'd reach for robust standard errors in that case rather than trusting the default OLS output blindly.
commonMistakes: Treating 'BLUE' as 'best possible estimator, full stop' rather than best among linear, unbiased estimators specifically
Assuming OLS's point estimate becomes biased the moment any Gauss-Markov assumption fails (bias specifically comes from violating exogeneity, not homoscedasticity or autocorrelation)
Not knowing that violated homoscedasticity/autocorrelation assumptions corrupt standard errors specifically, requiring robust SEs
keyPoints: Gauss-Markov theorem: OLS is BLUE under its five assumptions
BLUE = best among linear, unbiased estimators -- not best among all possible estimators
Violating exogeneity biases the coefficient itself; violating homoscedasticity/no-autocorrelation corrupts standard errors, not necessarily the coefficient
Robust (White/Newey-West) standard errors fix the SE problem without needing a different point estimator

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly and precisely states what BLUE guarantees
Correctly explains what it does NOT guarantee
Distinguishes which assumption violations affect bias vs. standard errors

questions.title: Why Minimum-Variance Portfolios Never Get Stuck in a Local Minimum
questions.prompt: Explain why the minimum-variance portfolio optimization problem never has a 'bad' local minimum that isn't also the global minimum, and name the specific property of the covariance matrix that makes this true.
questions.modelAnswer: Portfolio variance, f(w) = w^T*Sigma*w, is a convex function because its Hessian is simply 2*Sigma (constant everywhere), and a covariance matrix Sigma is always symmetric positive semi-definite by construction -- every variance is non-negative, so w^T*Sigma*w >= 0 for all w, which is exactly the Hessian test for convexity. For a convex function minimized over a convex feasible set (the budget and return constraints in a minimum-variance problem are linear/affine, keeping the set convex), there is a theorem guaranteeing every local minimum is also the global minimum -- there's no risk of gradient descent or the Lagrangian method finding a stationary point that's only locally, not globally, optimal. This is why the minimum-variance problem has one clean, provably optimal closed-form answer, not several competing candidate solutions to compare.
questions.professionalAnswer: The short answer is: portfolio variance is a convex function, full stop, and that single fact is what saves you from ever worrying about local minima here. It's convex because its Hessian is just 2*Sigma, and a covariance matrix is always positive semi-definite -- that's not a special property of any particular Sigma, it's true of every covariance matrix by construction, since it ultimately just reflects the fact that a variance can never be negative. Once you know the objective is convex and the constraints are linear (so the feasible set is convex too), there's a clean theorem that any local minimum you find IS the global minimum -- no multi-start, no second-guessing, which is exactly why the minimum-variance portfolio has one clean closed-form answer and not several candidates to compare.
commonMistakes: Treating convexity as a special feature of this particular problem rather than a general consequence of Sigma always being PSD
Confusing convexity (guarantees local=global min) with strict convexity (needed for a unique solution)
Assuming other portfolio objectives, like maximizing the Sharpe ratio, automatically share this same guarantee (they generally don't)
keyPoints: A function is convex if its Hessian is positive semi-definite everywhere
Portfolio variance's Hessian is 2*Sigma, and Sigma is always PSD by construction
Convex objective + convex feasible set => any local minimum is the global minimum
This is why minimum-variance has one clean, provably optimal solution
Sharpe-ratio maximization does NOT share this guarantee -- it's generally nonconvex

Correctly states the local-minimum-is-global-minimum guarantee for convex problems

questions.title: The Four Properties That Define Brownian Motion
questions.prompt: List the four defining properties of standard Brownian motion, and explain why these make it a natural starting point for modeling a stock's log-price, despite the fact that Brownian motion is nowhere differentiable.
questions.modelAnswer: Standard Brownian motion W_t satisfies four properties: (1) W_0 = 0; (2) independent increments -- non-overlapping time intervals' changes are mutually independent; (3) Gaussian increments -- W_t - W_s ~ N(0, t-s), so Var(W_t) = t; (4) continuous paths, with no jumps. It's nowhere differentiable because over a tiny interval of length dt, the increment has standard deviation sqrt(dt), so the 'slope' (increment/dt) has standard deviation sqrt(dt)/dt = 1/sqrt(dt), which blows up to infinity as dt -> 0. Despite not being differentiable, it's still a natural starting point for a stock's log-price because the independent-increments property models the idea that new information arrives unpredictably and independently of the past (consistent with the Efficient Market Hypothesis), and the Var(W_t)=t scaling exactly matches the sqrt(t)-scaling seen in the discrete random walk this process is the continuous-time limit of.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd list the four properties plainly: starts at zero, independent increments, Gaussian increments with variance equal to the elapsed time, and continuous (no-jump) paths. The nowhere-differentiable part sounds like it should disqualify it from being useful, but it doesn't -- the reason it's non-differentiable is that the variance of an increment only shrinks like sqrt(dt), not like dt itself, so the implied 'instantaneous slope' never settles down to a finite number. That's a real mathematical quirk, but it doesn't stop Brownian motion from being exactly the right building block for a stock's log-price: independent increments is the mathematical expression of 'today's news is unrelated to yesterday's,' and the Var(W_t)=t scaling is precisely the random-walk scaling you'd expect a price process built from lots of small, independent shocks to have.
commonMistakes: Assuming a continuous path must also be differentiable, which is false for Brownian motion specifically
Forgetting independent increments is what gives Brownian motion its Markov-like, memoryless character
Conflating Brownian motion itself (W_t) with geometric Brownian motion (the exponential model actually used for prices)
keyPoints: W_0=0, independent increments, Gaussian increments with Var(W_t)=t, continuous paths
Nowhere differentiable because the increment's standard deviation scales like sqrt(dt), not dt
Independent increments models unpredictable, memoryless arrival of new information
Var(W_t)=t matches the sqrt(t) standard-deviation scaling from the discrete random walk
W_t itself is the building block; GBM is the actual model used for stock prices

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly lists all four defining properties
Correctly explains why it's nowhere differentiable
Connects the properties to why it's a natural modeling starting point

questions.title: Computing a Rank-1 Approximation of a Return Matrix with SVD
questions.prompt: Given a NumPy matrix X of centered daily returns for several assets, write the code to compute its SVD and build the best rank-1 approximation of X. Briefly explain in what sense this approximation is 'best.'
questions.modelAnswer: U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False) gives the singular values in S (descending order) and the singular vectors in U's columns and Vt's rows. The best rank-1 approximation is rank1 = S[0] * np.outer(U[:, 0], Vt[0, :]). This is 'best' in the precise sense of the Eckart-Young theorem: among every possible rank-1 matrix, this specific one minimizes the Frobenius-norm (least-squares) reconstruction error against X -- no other rank-1 matrix gets numerically closer to X than this one does.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code is short: thin SVD with full_matrices=False, then just take the first singular value and the first columns/rows of U and Vt and multiply them back together as an outer product. The 'best' claim isn't marketing language -- it's a specific, provable fact (the Eckart-Young theorem) that this exact construction minimizes the sum of squared reconstruction errors among every possible rank-1 matrix you could use to approximate X. In practice, how good that approximation actually looks depends on how much bigger S[0] is than S[1]; if the first singular value dominates, the rank-1 approximation captures most of X's real structure.
questions.example: rank1_approx = S[0] * np.outer(U[:, 0], Vt[0, :]) reproduces most of X's structure whenever S[0] is substantially larger than S[1], exactly the situation PCA exploits when discarding later components as noise.
commonMistakes: Forgetting full_matrices=False, which returns unnecessarily large U/Vt matrices for a non-square X
Using S as if it were already a full diagonal matrix with matching shape, rather than a 1D array of singular values
Treating 'best approximation' as 'exact reconstruction' rather than a least-squares-optimal approximation
keyPoints: np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False) returns U, S (1D), Vt
Rank-1 approximation: S[0] * np.outer(U[:,0], Vt[0,:])
Eckart-Young theorem: this minimizes the Frobenius-norm reconstruction error among all rank-1 matrices
Approximation quality depends on how dominant S[0] is relative to the other singular values

Correctly explains the Eckart-Young optimality sense of 'best'

questions.title: Fitting and Constraining a Random Forest on Noisy Financial Features

# X_train, y_train assumed already prepared
questions.modelAnswer: model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=6, min_samples_leaf=30, max_features="sqrt", random_state=0, n_jobs=-1); model.fit(X_train, y_train). questions.title: Ridge vs. Lasso on a Collinear Set of Momentum Features
questions.prompt: You have five momentum features (5-day, 10-day, 20-day, 40-day, 60-day lookbacks) that are highly correlated with each other. Write the sklearn code to fit both a Ridge and a Lasso model on standardized versions of these features, and explain which one you'd expect to behave more erratically here, and why.
questions.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

ridge_model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1.0))
lasso_model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=0.01, max_iter=10000))
ridge_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
lasso_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
questions.modelAnswer: Both are fit as shown, always with StandardScaler first since both penalties operate on coefficient magnitude and need features on comparable scales. Lasso is expected to behave more erratically here: with five highly correlated momentum lookbacks, Lasso's L1 penalty tends to arbitrarily pick one member of the correlated group and zero out the rest, so a small change in the training window can flip which specific lookback 'wins' the selection, producing an unstable, jumpy set of nonzero coefficients across refits. Ridge's L2 penalty, in contrast, shrinks all five coefficients together rather than selecting among them, which keeps its behavior far more stable under this kind of collinearity.
questions.professionalAnswer: Both get wrapped in a StandardScaler pipeline first -- that's not optional, since Ridge and Lasso both penalize coefficient size, and five features on wildly different natural scales would get penalized unevenly otherwise. With five lookbacks that are all measuring roughly the same thing, Lasso's feature-selection behavior means it tends to grab one of them more or less arbitrarily and zero out the other four -- and which one it grabs can flip between refits on slightly different data. Ridge doesn't try to select at all; it shrinks all five together, so its coefficients stay comparatively stable even though none of them get set to exactly zero.

questions.title: Simulating Geometric Brownian Motion Paths in NumPy
questions.prompt: Write the NumPy code to simulate 10,000 one-year GBM price paths for a stock starting at $100 with annual drift 8% and volatility 25%, using 252 daily steps. Then explain why you must use (mu - 0.5*sigma^2) as the drift term in the log-price, not mu itself.
questions.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
S0, mu, sigma, T, n_steps, n_paths = 100.0, 0.08, 0.25, 1.0, 252, 10_000
dt = T / n_steps
questions.modelAnswer: Z = rng.normal(size=(n_paths, n_steps)); log_increments = (mu - 0.5*sigma**2)*dt + sigma*np.sqrt(dt)*Z; log_price = np.log(S0) + np.cumsum(log_increments, axis=1); S = np.exp(log_price). The -0.5*sigma^2 term is required because applying Ito's lemma to f(S)=ln(S) under the GBM dynamics dS=mu*S*dt+sigma*S*dW produces exactly this correction: d(ln S) = (mu - 0.5*sigma^2)*dt + sigma*dW, not the naive d(ln S)=mu*dt+sigma*dW you'd get from substituting dS/S directly as if this were ordinary calculus. Using mu alone would systematically overstate the expected log-return, biasing every simulated price path upward relative to the correct GBM solution.
questions.professionalAnswer: Code-wise: draw standard normal shocks Z of shape (n_paths, n_steps), build log_increments using (mu - 0.5*sigma**2)*dt + sigma*sqrt(dt)*Z, cumulative-sum them, add log(S0), then exponentiate to get the price paths back. The -0.5*sigma^2 isn't an arbitrary adjustment -- it's the direct output of Ito's lemma applied to ln(S): because Brownian motion has nonzero quadratic variation, the chain rule picks up an extra second-order term that ordinary calculus wouldn't have, and dropping it (which is exactly what happens if you naively substitute mu as the log-price drift) biases every simulated path's expected growth upward.

cumsum the log-increments, add log(S0), then np.exp to recover price paths

Omitting it (using mu alone) biases the simulated price distribution upward

questions.title: Flagging Implausible Ticks Without Removing Real Crashes
questions.prompt: Write the pandas/NumPy code to flag implausible price ticks in a return series using a rolling median and median absolute deviation (MAD), and explain why this is safer than simply dropping any return beyond 3 standard deviations from a rolling mean.
questions.code:
import numpy as np

def flag_bad_ticks(returns, window=21, mad_threshold=8):
    rolling_median = returns.rolling(window, center=True).median()
    abs_dev = (returns - rolling_median).abs()
    mad = abs_dev.rolling(window, center=True).median()
    robust_z = 0.6745 * (returns - rolling_median) / mad.replace(0, np.nan)
    return robust_z.abs() > mad_threshold
questions.modelAnswer: flag_bad_ticks(log_returns) returns a boolean mask of implausible points using a robust z-score built from the rolling median and MAD, scaled by 0.6745 to make it comparable to a standard deviation under normality. This is safer than a 3-standard-deviation rule on a rolling mean/std because the mean and standard deviation are themselves distorted by the very outliers you're trying to detect -- a single huge move drags the rolling mean and inflates the rolling std, which can mask the outlier itself or falsely flag subsequent ordinary moves as outliers. The median and MAD are robust statistics, barely affected by a handful of extreme points, so they give a much more reliable baseline to measure deviations against.
questions.professionalAnswer: The function itself: rolling median and rolling MAD (median of absolute deviations from that rolling median), then a robust z-score scaled by 0.6745 so it's comparable to an ordinary standard-deviation-based z-score. The key reason this beats a 3-sigma-on-rolling-mean/std rule is almost circular but important: mean and standard deviation are exactly the statistics an outlier distorts the most, so using them to detect the outlier is self-defeating -- one huge move drags the mean and inflates the std, which can make the very point you're trying to catch look less extreme than it is, or make perfectly normal subsequent points look falsely suspicious. Median and MAD don't have that problem; a handful of extreme points barely moves them.
commonMistakes: Using a low/aggressive MAD threshold that ends up flagging real fat-tail moves as 'bad data,' when large moves are a normal feature of return distributions
Auto-dropping every flagged point instead of routing them to manual review, since a flagged point can be real news (an earnings surprise) rather than a data error
Using mean/standard deviation instead of median/MAD, falling into the self-distorting-statistic trap this approach avoids
keyPoints: Rolling median and MAD are robust statistics, barely affected by the outliers they're meant to detect
A mean/std-based threshold is self-defeating since outliers distort the mean and std themselves
robust_z = 0.6745 * (x - rolling_median) / mad makes the robust z-score comparable to an ordinary one
A high threshold (e.g. 8) is deliberate, to avoid flagging legitimately large but real moves
Flagged points need manual review, not automatic removal

questions.title: Running the Jarque-Bera Test on a Return Series
questions.prompt: Write the scipy code to compute the skewness, excess kurtosis, and Jarque-Bera test statistic for a series of daily log returns, and explain what a significant Jarque-Bera result actually confirms about the data.
questions.code:
from scipy import stats

# log_returns: a NumPy array or pandas Series of daily log returns
questions.modelAnswer: skewness = stats.skew(log_returns); excess_kurt = stats.kurtosis(log_returns); jb_stat, jb_pvalue = stats.jarque_bera(log_returns). A significant (low p-value) Jarque-Bera result formally confirms that the sample's skewness and/or kurtosis deviate enough from the normal distribution's values (0 and 3) that the data is very unlikely to have come from a true normal distribution. It's a joint test of both moments at once, giving a precise statistical statement rather than just an eyeballed skew/kurtosis number -- backing up quantitatively what the skew/kurtosis figures usually already suggest for real financial returns.
questions.professionalAnswer: Three lines: stats.skew, stats.kurtosis, and stats.jarque_bera, all from scipy.stats. The useful thing to know about what Jarque-Bera actually confirms: it's a formal joint hypothesis test that the sample's skewness and kurtosis match what you'd expect from a true normal distribution; a significant (low p-value) result means that combination of skew and kurtosis is unlikely to have arisen from genuinely normal data, which for real daily financial returns is almost always the case. It doesn't tell you anything beyond that -- it's not testing for autocorrelation or any other property, just the shape of the marginal distribution via its third and fourth moments.

Treating a non-significant Jarque-Bera result as proof of normality, rather than just a failure to reject it
Running the test on raw prices instead of returns, which would fail for entirely different (non-stationarity) reasons

Jarque-Bera jointly tests whether skewness and kurtosis match a normal distribution's
A significant (low p-value) result confirms non-normality quantitatively
This should be run on log returns, not raw prices

questions.title: Plotting ACF on Returns vs. Squared Returns
questions.prompt: Write the statsmodels code to plot the ACF of daily log returns and separately the ACF of squared daily log returns, and explain why you'd expect these two plots to look completely different even though they come from the same data.
questions.code:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf

# log_returns: a pandas Series of daily log returns, already stationary
questions.modelAnswer: plot_acf(log_returns, lags=20); plot_acf(log_returns**2, lags=20). The plain-return ACF is expected to look nearly flat/insignificant at almost every lag beyond the very shortest, consistent with weak-form market efficiency -- little linear predictability in the direction of returns. The squared-return ACF, by contrast, is expected to show strong, slowly decaying autocorrelation, which is the statistical signature of volatility clustering: large moves (of either sign) tend to be followed by more large moves, so squared returns (a proxy for the magnitude of movement) are predictable even though the returns' own direction isn't. This is exactly the pattern GARCH-family models are built to capture.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two calls to plot_acf, once on the raw returns and once on the squared returns. The reason these look so different despite coming from the same series: return direction and return magnitude are different things statistically. The direction (sign and size) of tomorrow's return is barely related to today's -- that's the near-flat ACF on raw returns, and it's basically what weak-form market efficiency predicts. But the MAGNITUDE of moves clusters -- a volatile day tends to be followed by more volatile days -- and squaring the returns isolates exactly that magnitude signal, which is why its ACF decays slowly instead of looking flat. It's not a contradiction; it's two different questions about the same series.
commonMistakes: Expecting the squared-return ACF to look the same (flat) as the plain-return ACF
Concluding 'no autocorrelation in returns' means there's no predictable structure in the series at all -- volatility is still predictable
Forgetting to dropna() after computing log returns before plotting the ACF

Plain-return ACF: near-flat/insignificant at most lags, consistent with weak-form efficiency
Squared-return ACF: strong, slowly decaying autocorrelation -- the fingerprint of volatility clustering
This is exactly the structure GARCH-family models are designed to capture

questions.title: A Backtest Universe Built from Today's S&P 500 List
questions.prompt: A junior researcher builds a 20-year backtest universe by taking today's S&P 500 constituent list and pulling historical prices for exactly those companies. What's wrong with this approach, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This silently excludes every company that was removed from the index over those 20 years -- companies that went bankrupt, were acquired, were delisted, or underperformed and got dropped -- which were disproportionately the bad performers. The resulting backtest's universe only ever contains names that survived to today, which systematically inflates the measured historical returns relative to what an investor actually following the index over that period would have earned. This is classic survivorship bias. The fix: use a survivorship-bias-free, point-in-time database that reconstructs the actual index membership as of each historical date, retaining delisted names with their real (often poor) final returns recorded, rather than projecting today's membership backward.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem is that 'today's list, projected backward' quietly throws away every company that didn't make it -- bankruptcies, buyouts, delistings, underperformers that got dropped -- and those are specifically the bad outcomes, not a random sample. So the backtest ends up only ever seeing survivors, which makes historical performance look better than it really was. The fix isn't complicated in concept, just in sourcing: you need a point-in-time, survivorship-bias-free dataset that tells you exactly who was actually in the index on each historical date, including the names that later disappeared, with their real returns intact up to whenever they left.
commonMistakes: Assuming today's constituent list is close enough to accurate for history too
Not recognizing that delistings/bankruptcies are disproportionately bad performers, so their exclusion specifically inflates measured returns
Conflating survivorship bias with look-ahead bias -- related but distinct problems
keyPoints: Today's constituent list is not the same as the historical constituent list on any past date
Delisted/failed companies vanish from naive datasets, and they're disproportionately bad performers
This systematically inflates backtested returns -- it's not a neutral simplification
The fix is point-in-time, survivorship-bias-free data reconstructing actual historical membership

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses survivorship bias
Explains why the bias specifically inflates returns (disproportionate exclusion of bad performers)
Proposes the point-in-time data fix

questions.title: A -50% 'Return' That Was Actually a Stock Split
questions.prompt: A return-calculation script flags a stock as having lost 50% of its value overnight, triggering a risk alert. Investigating, you find the stock did a 2-for-1 split that day and nothing else unusual happened. What went wrong, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: The script computed returns on unadjusted (raw) close prices. A 2-for-1 split halves the raw quoted price overnight with zero change in the company's actual value or any shareholder's actual wealth, so a naive pct_change() on unadjusted prices sees half/full - 1 = -50% and records a fake catastrophic loss that never happened economically. The fix is to compute returns on an adjusted close series that's back-adjusted for the split (and similarly for dividends), so the split is priced in consistently across the whole history rather than creating a one-day artificial discontinuity in the raw series.
questions.professionalAnswer: The root cause is using the wrong price field: raw 'close,' not an adjusted close, which means a 2-for-1 split -- which halves the quoted price but changes nothing real about the company's value -- gets read by the return calculation as an actual 50% crash. The fix is to switch the pipeline to compute returns off the adjusted close series, which has already been back-adjusted for exactly this kind of corporate action, so splits and dividend payments don't show up as fake price discontinuities. I'd also add this as a standing sanity check: anything the risk alert flags should be cross-checked against a corporate-actions calendar before anyone treats it as a real move.
commonMistakes: Using raw 'close' instead of 'adj_close' for return calculations, which breaks across any split or dividend event
Assuming a vendor's 'adjusted' field already handles both splits and dividends, when it may only cover one of the two
Not having an automated cross-check against a corporate-actions calendar before a large single-day move triggers a false alarm
keyPoints: Unadjusted prices create fake overnight jumps/drops around stock splits
A 2-for-1 split halves the raw price with zero real change in value
The fix is computing returns on a properly back-adjusted close series
Always confirm exactly what a vendor's 'adjusted' field actually adjusts for

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the unadjusted-price bug behind the fake -50% return
Proposes the adjusted-close fix clearly

questions.title: A Model That 'Explains' a Random Walk Suspiciously Well
questions.prompt: You fit an AR(1) model to a raw (unadjusted) price series and get a suspiciously high R-squared, with a coefficient near 1.0. What's actually happening here, and why does this result tell you almost nothing useful about the series?
questions.modelAnswer: A price series behaves like a random walk, X_t = X_(t-1) + eps_t, so an AR(1) fit will naturally find a coefficient near 1.0 and a very high R-squared simply because tomorrow's price level tends to be close to today's -- not because the model found any real predictive structure. This is the classic hallmark of fitting a model to a non-stationary, unit-root series: the fit looks great by a naive R-squared standard, but it's purely an artifact of the series' own persistence (today's level is a good 'predictor' of tomorrow's level precisely because prices don't jump around much relative to their own size day to day), not genuine forecasting skill. The fix is to difference the series -- work with returns instead of price levels -- before fitting, and to treat any suspiciously high R-squared on price levels with immediate suspicion rather than excitement.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's actually happening: a coefficient near 1.0 in an AR(1) is exactly the signature of a unit-root, random-walk process, and the high R-squared that comes with it is a well-known statistical mirage, not a real finding -- prices move slowly relative to their own level day to day, so 'tomorrow's price is close to today's price' is trivially a great predictor, but it's not telling you anything useful or tradeable. I'd flag this result as a red flag, not a win, and the fix is to refit on returns (the differenced series) instead of raw price levels, where a coefficient near 1.0 and a high R-squared would actually mean something.
commonMistakes: Treating a high R-squared on price levels as evidence of real predictive skill
Not recognizing an AR(1) coefficient near 1.0 as the textbook signature of a unit-root/random-walk process
Fitting AR-family models to prices out of habit instead of returns
keyPoints: An AR(1) coefficient near 1.0 signals a unit root, not genuine predictability
The resulting high R-squared on price levels is a well-known statistical artifact
This reflects the series' own persistence, not any real forecasting skill
Always difference (use returns) and test stationarity before trusting an AR-family model's fit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the unit-root / spurious-fit artifact
Explains why the high R-squared is misleading rather than meaningful

questions.title: Residuals That Still Show a Spike in the ACF
questions.prompt: After fitting an ARMA model, you plot the ACF of the residuals and see a statistically significant spike at lag 5. What does this tell you about the model, and what should you do next?
questions.modelAnswer: A correctly specified time-series model should leave residuals that look like white noise -- no remaining autocorrelation at any lag. A significant spike at lag 5 means the model is under-specified: there's still real, systematic structure in the data at that lag the current (p,d,q) order hasn't captured. The next step is to formally confirm this with a Ljung-Box test (which should reject the 'no autocorrelation' null jointly across the relevant lags), and then revisit the model order -- trying additional AR or MA terms that could plausibly capture a lag-5 effect (for example, a weekly pattern in daily data) -- re-running the same diagnostic after each refit rather than assuming one fix is automatically sufficient.
questions.professionalAnswer: That spike is the model telling you it's not done yet: a well-specified model's residuals shouldn't have any visible structure left, and a significant lag-5 spike means there's real autocorrelation the current order missed. I'd formally check it with a Ljung-Box test rather than relying on the visual spike alone, and then go back to the identification step -- in daily data a lag-5 effect often points at something weekly, so that's a reasonable first place to look for an additional AR or MA term. The important discipline is re-running the same residual check after any refit, not stopping once the first visible spike is addressed.
commonMistakes: Treating a single visible ACF spike as 'probably just noise' without a formal Ljung-Box test
Not considering that a lag-5 effect in daily data might reflect a weekly pattern
Stopping model refinement once AIC/BIC look reasonable, without ever checking the residuals
keyPoints: Well-specified model residuals should look like white noise -- no leftover autocorrelation
A significant ACF spike at a given lag signals the model is under-specified at that lag
The Ljung-Box test formally confirms whether leftover autocorrelation is statistically significant
The fix is to revisit model order and re-diagnose, not to ignore the signal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the residual structure as under-specification
Proposes a Ljung-Box test to formally confirm it
Proposes revisiting model order with a plausible explanation (e.g. weekly pattern)

questions.title: Picking an ARIMA Order by BIC Alone, Then Seeing It Fail
questions.prompt: A colleague grid-searched dozens of (p,d,q) combinations and picked the one with the lowest BIC, with no residual check afterward. The model then forecasts poorly out-of-sample. What's the most likely issue with this workflow, and what step was skipped?
questions.modelAnswer: AIC and BIC only measure a tradeoff between in-sample fit and model complexity -- they say nothing directly about whether a model is actually well-specified or forecasts well out-of-sample. Picking purely by lowest BIC skips the 'diagnose' step of the Box-Jenkins identify-estimate-diagnose workflow: the residuals of the 'best BIC' model were never checked with a Ljung-Box test or visual inspection for leftover autocorrelation, trend, or changing variance. A model can have the lowest BIC among an entire search grid and still leave clear structure in its residuals, and that kind of misspecification is exactly the sort of thing that shows up later as poor out-of-sample forecasts, even though the in-sample fit statistic looked fine.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway here is 'no residual check afterward' -- that's the missing step, full stop. AIC and BIC are useful for narrowing a search grid down to good candidates, but they're purely in-sample fit-versus-complexity measures; they don't verify the model is actually well-specified. The Box-Jenkins workflow has three steps -- identify, estimate, diagnose -- and this process stopped after estimate. I'd go back and run Ljung-Box and a residual ACF plot on the chosen model before trusting it with anything, and only then validate it genuinely out-of-sample.
commonMistakes: Treating information-criterion minimization as the final step rather than a way to narrow down candidates
Skipping residual diagnostics (Ljung-Box, ACF plot) entirely after model selection
Not validating the selected model against genuine out-of-sample data before trusting it
keyPoints: AIC/BIC balance in-sample fit against model complexity, not forecast quality
Box-Jenkins has three steps: identify, estimate, diagnose -- diagnose was skipped
A model can have the lowest BIC in a search grid and still leave structure in its residuals
Residual checks (Ljung-Box, ACF) and genuine out-of-sample validation are the real tests of model quality

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing diagnose step as the issue
Correctly explains what AIC/BIC do and do not measure
